summary: Defines a NAMESPACE command for IMAP4 that lets a client discover the prefixes servers use for personal mailboxes, other users' mailboxes, and shared mailboxes.

eli5.summary: A command that asks the mail server where each kind of mailbox lives, such as yours, other people's and shared ones.

questions: how do imap clients find shared mailboxes
what is the imap namespace command
what are personal and shared namespaces in imap
what does namespace nil mean in imap
subtitle: A one-command way for an IMAP client to learn where a server keeps your mailboxes and everyone else's.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 defines no default server namespace, so servers present mailboxes in different layouts and users had to type prefixes such as #shared by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The NAMESPACE command returns the prefix and hierarchy delimiter for the server's personal, other users' and shared namespaces, with NIL for any class that is not available.
tldr.outcome: Clients can find where to create mailboxes like Sent Mail and how to reach shared mailboxes without manual configuration. A later RFC 4466 updates this document.

today: RFC 2342 is a Proposed Standard published in May 1998 and has been updated by RFC 4466. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Namespace Command
sections.content:
IMAP4 (RFC 2060) does not define a default server namespace. Two models grew up. In the Personal Mailbox model the default view holds only the user's own mailboxes, and shared ones need an escape mechanism. In the Complete Hierarchy model the default view also includes every other mailbox the user can reach.

Both models make life hard for clients. A client that wants to create a mailbox for sent mail or drafts needs to know the personal prefix, and the user had to type it in. Users also had to type prefixes such as #shared to see shared mailboxes. RFC 2342 adds a NAMESPACE command so the client can discover all of this automatically.
sections.eli5: Different mail servers organise their folders differently, like houses with different floor plans. This command is a map the server hands to your mail program.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Namespace
sections.content:
The RFC defines three namespace classes. The Personal Namespace is the part the server considers within the personal scope of the authenticated user; if an INBOX exists it MUST appear here, and normally there SHOULD be only one. The Other Users' Namespace holds mailboxes from other people's personal namespaces, and the user must be explicitly granted access. A common case is a manager granting a secretary access. The Shared Namespace holds mailboxes meant to be shared among users that do not live in anyone's personal namespace.

The namespaces a server uses MAY differ from user to user. A server may also expose only a subset of the namespaces it supports, so a client SHOULD let the user type a namespace prefix manually.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of shelves: your own shelf, shelves belonging to other people who let you look, and a public shelf for everyone.

sections.title: The NAMESPACE Command
sections.content:
A server that supports the extension MUST list the keyword NAMESPACE in its CAPABILITY response. The command takes no arguments and is valid in the Authenticated and Selected states. It may finish with OK, NO or BAD.

The server answers with one untagged NAMESPACE response containing, in order, the personal, other users' and shared namespaces. Each entry gives a prefix and a hierarchy delimiter. A class that is not available is sent as NIL. The response MAY carry extensions, and any extension not on the IETF standards track MUST be prefixed with X-.

With the prefix a client can, for example, create a personal mailbox. If a server shows the prefix INBOX. with delimiter ., the client creates INBOX.Sent Mail. Servers may have several personal namespaces, and a client MUST be prepared for that. When it is unclear where to create a mailbox, the client SHOULD let the user choose.
sections.eli5: You ask one short question and the server answers with three lists: yours, other people's and shared. An empty list says 'none of those here'.

sections.title: Reading the Responses and Other Users' Mailboxes
sections.content:
The RFC gives nine examples. In the first, a server has one personal namespace with no prefix and / as delimiter. In another, an anonymous user has no personal mailboxes, so the personal and other-users entries are NIL and the shared namespace needs no prefix. A further example shows that the delimiter can differ between namespaces.

The level after the other users' prefix SHOULD be a <username> as used with IMAP4 LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE. A client can append % to the prefix in a LIST command to see which users are available. A server SHOULD NOT return users who have not granted access, and MAY return only users who have, or MAY answer NO so that the client must include a user name in the prefix. A prefix might also contain no delimiter at all, such as ~.

Historically namespaces began with the hash character, which must be written as %23 in IMAP URLs. Implementers MAY therefore choose prefixes without it.
sections.eli5: If you want to peek at a friend's shelf, you ask for a list of friends who allowed it. A careful server may only tell you once you name the friend yourself.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The grammar uses ABNF. The command is simply NAMESPACE. The response is "*" SP "NAMESPACE" SP followed by three namespace values: the first is the personal namespace(s), the second the other users' namespace(s), the third the shared namespace(s). Each value is either nil or a parenthesised list of entries made of a string prefix and either a quoted character delimiter or nil, plus optional response extensions.

Because a namespace prefix names a mailbox, any international string in the response MUST use the modified UTF-7 format from RFC 2060.
sections.eli5: The syntax is the exact spelling rule for the server's answer, so every mail program reads it the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: When a client sends LIST with the other users' prefix, a server SHOULD NOT list users who have not granted list access to the current user. Doing so could disclose confidential information about who is on the server, or hand an attacker a starting list of user accounts to attack.
sections.eli5: A server should not read out the names of everyone who has an account, because that would help a snoop pick targets.

data.title: Personal, other users' and shared namespaces
data.code:
C: A001 NAMESPACE
S: * NAMESPACE (("" "/")) (("~" "/")) (("#shared/" "/")
   ("#public/" "/")("#ftp/" "/")("#news." "."))
S: A001 OK NAMESPACE command completed
